books.title: User Story Mapping: Discover the Whole Story, Build the Right Product
practices: Tell the user's journey left to right before you prioritize down.
A flat backlog hides the product; a map restores the whole story.
Slice a walking skeleton that is end-to-end thin, not a layer cake of plumbing.
Stories are invitations to a conversation, not mini specifications.
Release slices should be valuable to a real user, not only internally complete.
Do not map features; map activities and tasks the person already does.
Shared understanding beats signed documents as the output of mapping.
Split by stepping through the journey, not by splitting nouns into CRUD.
The map goes stale; redraw when the journey changes.
This is stepping, not a promise of velocity.

books.title: User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development
practices: Write stories as valuable increments with a user role and a reason.
Independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable is a hygiene check, not a religion.
Gather stories from roles, not only from a single proxy.
Acceptance tests belong with the story or the story is unfinished as a step.
Epics are placeholders; they are not work.
Do not treat 'as a user' as a template zombie; name the role.
Split when the story hides multiple steps or multiple users.
Estimates are for sequencing conversations, not for contracts.
Stories that only the database can love are not user stories.
Pair with mapping so the pile of cards still has a plot.

books.title: Shape Up: Stop Running in Circles and Ship Work that Matters
practices: Shape work before you bet: problem, appetite, solution outline, rabbit holes, no-gos.
Appetite is a time budget, not a feature tax.
A pitch is a bet, not a backlog forever-item.
Fixed time, variable scope inside the appetite.
Cool-down exists so the next bet is shaped, not improvised.
Do not start a cycle with unshaped wishes.
Hill charts show unknown-to-known, not percent-complete theater.
Circuit breakers: if the bet cannot land in the appetite, cut scope or stop.
Shaping is not a 200-page spec; it is a boundary with fat marker strokes.
Refuse circles of status meetings that replace shipping steps.

books.title: The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development
books.reported_reason: Celeritas 2009; queues, batch size, WIP, cost of delay.
practices: Watch queues; invisible work-in-process is delay.
Smaller batches reduce variability and feedback time.
Cost of delay should sequence steps, not HiPPO urgency.
WIP limits are a stepping tool, not a punishment.
Cadence and synchronization beat heroic integration weeks.
Do not optimize utilization of people at the expense of flow.
Decentralize control where information is local; centralize where it is not.
Variability is not always waste; some of it is the search.
Measure flow time of a slice, not only story points burned.
This is economics of stepping, not a new ceremony brand.
